farraa:61-61.t: His saying: ﴿إِنَّا لَمُدْرَكُونَ﴾ and ﴿لَمُدَّركُونَ﴾: [the latter is] of the pattern muftaʿalūn from al-idrāk (overtaking), just as you say ḥafartu and iḥtafartu with one and the same meaning. Likewise ﴿لَمُدْرَكُونَ﴾ and ﴿لَمُدَّرَكُونَ﴾ have one meaning, and Allah knows best.

farraa:77-77.t: His saying: ﴿فَإِنَّهُمْ عَدُوٌّ لِيۤ إِلاَّ رَبَّ ٱلْعَالَمِينَ﴾ that is: every god of yours I do not worship, except the Lord of the Worlds, for Him I worship. It is put in the accusative by exception (istithnāʾ), as though he said: they are an enemy, not worshipped, except the Lord of the Worlds, for Him I worship. And they only said ﴿فَإِنَّهُمْ عَدُوٌّ لِيۤ﴾ [Translator's note: so in the source, "they said"; the words are Ibrāhīm's], meaning: were I to worship them, they would be an opponent and an enemy to me on the Day of Resurrection.

farraa:84-84.t: His saying: ﴿وَٱجْعَل لِّي لِسَانَ صِدْقٍ فِي ٱلآخِرِينَ﴾: ʿAmr ibn Abī al-Miqdām related to me from al-Ḥakam from Mujāhid, who said: [it means] good praise (thanāʾan ḥasanan).

farraa:111-111.t: His saying: ﴿وَٱتَّبَعَكَ ٱلأَرْذَلُونَ﴾: It has been mentioned that one of the readers read: وأتباعك الأرذلونَ ("while your followers are the lowliest"), but I have not found it from the well-known readers, though it is a good reading (wajh ḥasan).

farraa:128-128.t: His saying: ﴿أَتَبْنُونَ بِكُلِّ رِيعٍ﴾ and (رَيْع) are two dialectal forms, like al-rīr and al-rār, which is thin, poor marrow. And you say rāʿa al-ṭaʿāmu (the food increased) when it has rayʿ (yield, increase).

farraa:129-129.t: His saying: ﴿وَتَتَّخِذُونَ مَصَانِعَ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَخْلُدُونَ﴾: its meaning is: so that you may live forever (kay-mā takhludū).

farraa:130-130.t: His saying: ﴿وَإِذَا بَطَشْتُمْ بَطَشْتُمْ جَبَّارِينَ﴾: you kill in anger. This is the view of al-Kalbī. Someone else said: (بَطَشْتُم جَبّارينَ) with the whip.

farraa:137-137.t: His saying: ﴿خُلُقُ ٱلأَوَّلِينَ﴾: The reading of al-Kisāʾī is (خَلْق الأوَّلِينَ). Al-Farrāʾ said: and my reading is (خَلَق الأولينَ) [Translator's note: so in the source; from what follows, al-Farrāʾ's own preference is evidently خُلُق]. Whoever reads (خَلْق) means: their fabrication (ikhtilāq) and their lying; and whoever reads ﴿خَلُق الأولينَ﴾ means: the custom of the ancients, i.e. what your father inherited from the first ones. The Arabs say: "Tell us the tales of al-khalq," which are the fabricated legends and the like; that is why I chose al-khuluq.

farraa:148-148.t: His saying: ﴿هَضِيمٌ﴾: he says: as long as it is in its kawāfīr, which is the spathe (al-ṭalʿ). The Arabs call the spathe al-kufurrā and al-kawāfīr; the singular of [kawāfīr] is kāfūra, and kufurrāt is the singular of al-kufurrā.

farraa:149-149.t: His saying: ﴿بُيُوتاً فَارِهِينَ﴾: skilful; and ﴿فَرِهينَ﴾: exultant and insolent (ashirīn).

farraa:153-153.t:
His saying: ﴿إِنَّمَآ أَنتَ مِنَ ٱلْمُسَحَّرِينَ﴾: They said to him: you are not an angel; you are only a human being like us [Translator's note: the source reads مثلها, "like it"; read مثلنا]. Al-musaḥḥar is the one who is hollow — as though, and Allah knows best, it is from your saying "your lungs (saḥr) have swelled", i.e. you eat food and drink and are nourished (tusaḥḥaru) by it and kept going (tuʿallalu). The poet said:
فإن تسألينا فيمن نحن فإنَّنَا * عصَافير مِنْ هَذَا الأنامِ المسَحَّر
(If you ask us who we are, we are sparrows of these mankind that are fed and beguiled.)
[134/b] He means: the one kept going and the one deceived. And we hold that al-sāḥir (the sorcerer) is taken from that.

farraa:155-155.t: His saying: ﴿لَّهَا شِرْبٌ﴾: she has a share of the water. Al-sharb and al-shurb are both maṣdars (verbal nouns). The Arabs have said: "The last of them is the least of them in drinking" — shurban, shirban and sharban.

farraa:166-166.t: His saying: ﴿وَتَذَرُونَ مَا خَلَقَ لَكُمْ رَبُّكُمْ مِّنْ أَزْوَاجِكُمْ﴾: [i.e.] what He made for you of the private parts. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh [ibn Masʿūd]: (ما أصلح لكم ربّكم) ("what your Lord made fit for you").

farraa:171-171.t:
His saying: ﴿إِلاَّ عَجُوزاً فِي ٱلْغَابِرِينَ﴾: al-ghābirūn are those who remain. From this is the saying of the poet, al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza:
لا تكْسَعِ الشَّوْل بأغبارهَا * إنَّكَ لا تَدْرى مَنِ الناتجُ
(Do not seal the udders of the dry she-camels with their remaining milk; you do not know who will deliver their young.)
Al-aghbār here means the remnants of milk in the udders of camels and others; its singular is ghubr. He said: and one of Banū Asad, namely Abū al-Qamqām, recited to me:
تَذُبُّ منها كُلَّ حَيزَبُونِ * مَانِعَةٍ لغُبْرِها زَبُونِ
(It drives off from them every old crone, withholding her remaining milk, a kicker.)

farraa:184-184.t: His saying: ﴿وَٱلْجِبِلَّةَ ٱلأَوَّلِينَ﴾: ʿĀṣim and al-Aʿmash read it with kasra on the jīm and a doubled lām, and others put it with ḍamma [on the jīm and bāʾ]; the lām is doubled in both views: ﴿والجُبُلّة﴾.

farraa:193-193.t: His saying: ﴿نَزَلَ بِهِ ٱلرُّوحُ ٱلأَمِينُ﴾: thus the readers read it. Al-Aʿmash, ʿĀṣim and al-Ḥasan read it (نَزَّلَ به) with the doubled form, and they put (الرُوحَ الأمِين) in the accusative — he is Jibrīl — ﴿عَلَى قَلْبِكَ﴾: he recites it to you. The people of Medina put ﴿الرُّوح الأمين﴾ in the nominative and read ﴿نَزل﴾ without doubling; both are the same in meaning.

farraa:196-196.t: His saying: ﴿وَإِنَّهُ لَفِي زُبُرِ ٱلأَوَّلِينَ﴾: and indeed this Qurʾān is in some of the scriptures of the ancients and their books. He said ﴿فى زُبُر﴾ while it is only in some of them, and that is allowable (wāsiʿ), for you say "the people went" when only some of them went.

farraa:197-197.t: His saying: ﴿أَوَ لَمْ يَكُن لَّهُمْ آيَةً أَن يَعْلَمَهُ عُلَمَاءُ بَنِيۤ إِسْرَائِيلَ﴾: he says: they know the knowledge of Muhammad ﷺ, that he is a prophet, in their scripture. (الآية) is accusative and (أنْ) is in the position of the nominative. Had you said ﴿أَوَ لَمْ يَكُن لَّهُمْ آيَةٌ﴾ in the nominative, (أن يعلمه), making (أن) in the position of the accusative, that would be permissible.

farraa:198-198.t: His saying: ﴿وَلَوْ نَزَّلْنَاهُ عَلَىٰ بَعْضِ ٱلأَعْجَمِينَ﴾: al-aʿjam is the one [impaired] in his tongue, while al-aʿjamī is the one attributed by his origin to the non-Arabs (العَجَم), even if he is eloquent. Whoever says aʿjam says ʿajmāʾ for a woman when she does not speak Arabic well. And it is permissible to say ʿajamī meaning aʿjamī, attributing him to his origin.

farraa:200-200.t:
His saying: ﴿كَذَلِكَ سَلَكْنَاهُ﴾: he says: We inserted denial (al-takdhīb) into the hearts of the criminals so that they would not believe in it ﴿حَتى يَرَوُا العَذَابَ الألِيمَ﴾. When the position of kay (in order that) in a construction like this is [filled by] (لا) together with an [implied] an, both the jussive and the nominative are sound after (لا). The Arabs say: "I tied up the horse lā yatafallat (so that it should not break loose)" in the jussive and the nominative, and "I bound the slave lā yafrir (so that he should not flee)" in the jussive and the nominative. It is put in the jussive only because its underlying sense is "if I do not tie it, it will flee", so it is put in the jussive according to the underlying sense. One of Banū ʿUqayl recited to me:
وحتى رأينا أحسن الفعل بيننا * مُسَاكتةَ لا يقرف الشرَّ قارف
(Until we saw that the best conduct between us was keeping silent, so that no one would commit evil.)
It is recited both in the nominative and the jussive. Another said:
لو كنت إذ جئتنا حَاولت رُؤْيتنَا * أو جئتنا مَاشياً لا يُعْرف الفرسُ
(Had you, when you came to us, sought to see us, or come to us on foot so that the horse would not be recognised…)
in the nominative and the jussive. And his saying:
لطالما حَلأنماها لا ترِدْ * فخلِّياها والسِّجالَ تبتردْ
(Long have we driven her from the water so that she should not drink; so leave her with the buckets to cool herself.)
is of that [type].

farraa:208-208.t: His saying: ﴿لاَّ لَهَا مُنذِرُونَ﴾ [Translator's note: the verse reads إِلاَّ لَهَا مُنذِرُونَ]; and in another place: ﴿إلاَ وَلَهَا كِتَابٌ معلوم﴾. This has already been explained.

farraa:209-209.t: His saying: ﴿ذِكْرَىٰ وَمَا كُنَّا ظَالِمِينَ﴾: ذِكْرى is in the position of the accusative, i.e. they warn them as a reminder (tadhkiratan) and a remembrance (dhikrā). Had you said (ذكرى) is in the position of the nominative, you would be right, i.e. "that is a reminder" or "this is a reminder".

farraa:210-210.t:
His saying: ﴿وَمَا تَنَزَّلَتْ بِهِ ٱلشَّيَاطِينُ﴾: you put the nūn in the nominative.
Al-Farrāʾ said: It has come from al-Ḥasan [as] (الشياطونَ), and it seems to be an error of the shaykh: he thought it was like al-muslimīn and al-muslimūn.

farraa:212-212.t: His saying: ﴿إِنَّهُمْ عَنِ ٱلسَّمْعِ لَمَعْزُولُونَ﴾: he means the devils, by the pelting of the stars.

farraa:218-219.t: His saying: ﴿يَرَاكَ حِينَ تَقُومُ﴾ ﴿وَتَقَلُّبَكَ فِي ٱلسَّاجِدِينَ﴾: he says: He sees your turning about [135/a] among those who pray. His turning about is his standing, his bowing and his prostration.

farraa:221-221.t: His saying: ﴿هَلْ أُنَبِّئُكُمْ عَلَىٰ مَن تَنَزَّلُ ٱلشَّيَاطِينُ﴾: Before they were pelted, the devils used to come to the soothsayers, such as Musaylima the Liar, Ṭulayḥa and Sajāḥ, and cast to them some of what they heard, and they lied. That is ﴿يُلْقُون﴾ to their soothsayers ﴿السَّمْعَ﴾ which they heard, ﴿وَأَكْثَرُهُمْ كَاذِبُونَ﴾.

farraa:224-224.t:
His saying: ﴿وَٱلشُّعَرَآءُ يَتَّبِعُهُمُ ٱلْغَاوُونَ﴾: it was revealed about Ibn al-Zabaʿrā and those like him, because they used to satirise the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims.
His saying: ﴿يَتَّبِعُهُمُ ٱلْغَاوُونَ﴾: their misguided ones, who approve of reviling the Prophet, upon him be peace.
Then He made an exception for the poets of the Muslims, saying: ﴿إلا الذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾.

farraa:227-227.t: His saying: ﴿إِلاَّ ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُواْ﴾: because they replied to them; that is His saying ﴿وَٱنتَصَرُواْ مِن بَعْدِ مَا ظُلِمُواْ﴾. It has been read ﴿يَتَّبِعُهُم الغاوون﴾ and ﴿يَتْبَعَهُم﴾, and each is correct.

farraa:3-3.t: His saying: ﴿بَاخِعٌ نَّفْسَكَ﴾ — killing yourself. ﴿أَلاَّ يَكُونُواْ مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ — the position of (أن) is accusative because it is conditional (jazāʾ), as though you said: if they do not believe, you will kill yourself. Since it is past, you gave (أن) fatḥa, as you say "I came to you because (an) you came to me". Had it not been past, you would say: "I will come to you if «[Translator's note: the source has «إلى» (to), apparently a misprint for «إن» (if).]» you come to me". And had it been jussive, with (إن) given kasra, it would be correct. Similar to it is Allah's saying ﴿وَلاَ يجْرِمَنّكم شَنَآنُ قَوْم أَنْ صَدُّوكُم﴾ and ﴿إن صَدُّوكم﴾; His saying ﴿من الشهدَاءِ أَن تَضِلّ﴾ and ﴿إِنْ تَضِلّ﴾; and likewise ﴿أَفَنَضْرِبُ عَنْكُمُ الذكرَ صَفْحاً إنْ كُنْتُم﴾ and ﴿أن كنتم﴾ — two good ways.

farraa:4-4.t:
His saying: ﴿إِن نَّشَأْ نُنَزِّلْ عَلَيْهِمْ مِّنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ آيَةً﴾ — then He said ﴿فظلَّت﴾ and did not say (فتَظللّ) as He said ﴿ننزل﴾. That is correct: to conjoin a faʿala [past] verb to the jussive of the conditional, because in a conditional faʿala is fit in the place of yafʿalu and yafʿalu in the place of faʿala. Do you not see that you say "If you visited me, I visited you" and "If you visit me, I will visit you", with one meaning? Therefore His saying ﴿فظلّت﴾ is fit, referred back to a yafʿalu. Likewise His saying ﴿تباركَ الذى إن شاء جَعَل لكَ خَيرا من ذلكَ جَنّات﴾, then He said ﴿ويَجْعَلْ لك قصُوراً﴾: He referred a yafʿalu back to [a faʿala], and that is equivalent to His referring (فظَلَّت) back to (نُنَزِّل). Likewise the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) of a conditional: yafʿalu is met with faʿala, and faʿala with yafʿalu, as in your saying (in qumta aqum, and in taqum qumtu). The best speech is to give a yafʿalu an answer like it and a faʿala an answer like it, as in your saying "If you trade (in tattajir), you will profit (tarbaḥ)", which is better than saying "If you trade, you profited (rabiḥta)". Likewise "If you traded, you profited" is better than saying "If you traded, you will profit". Both are permissible. Allah said ﴿مَنْ كَانَ يُرِيدُ الحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا وزينَتَها نُوَفِّ إليهم﴾: He said ﴿نُوَفّ﴾, and it is the answer to kāna. The poet said:
إن يَسمَعُوا سُبَّة طارُوا بهَا فَرَحاً * منى وما يَسَمَعُوا من صَالحٍ دَفَنُوا
(If they hear a disgrace of mine, they fly off with it in joy; and whatever good they hear [of me], they bury.)
He gave the answer with faʿala while before it was yafʿalu. Al-Farrāʾ said: (in yasmaʿū subbatan, on the pattern of ghayya).
His saying: ﴿فَظَلَّتْ أَعْنَاقُهُمْ لَهَا خَاضِعِينَ﴾ — the verb belongs to the necks, so someone may say: how is it that He did not say khāḍiʿatan? There are several explanations of that, all of them correct. The first is that Mujāhid took al-aʿnāq (the necks) to be the great men, so al-aʿnāq here is like your saying: their heads — the heads and great ones of the people — remained humbled before it, before the sign. The second explanation is that you take al-aʿnāq to be the groups, as you say "I saw the people [going] to so-and-so as one neck (ʿunuq)", so you take al-aʿnāq to be the groups and bands. Dearer to me than these two explanations in Arabic is that when the necks are humbled, their owners are humbled; so you first made the verb for the necks, then made (خَاضِعِينَ) for the men, as the poet said:
عَلَى قَبِضة مَوْجُوءة ظهرُ كَفّه * فلا المرْءُ مُسْتَحْىٍ ولا هو طَاعِمُ
(Over a handful [of food], the back of his hand beaten away — so the man is neither ashamed nor fed.)
He made the verb of "the back" feminine because the hand comprises the back and suffices for it, just as it suffices you to say "My neck has humbled itself to you". Do you not see that the Arabs say "Every possessor of an eye is looking (nāẓir, masc.) and looking (nāẓira, fem.) at you", because your saying "My eye looked at you" and "I looked at you" have one meaning? So (كُلّ), to which the verb belongs, was left aside, and [the verb] was referred to the eye. And had you said "fa-ẓallat aʿnāquhum lahā khāḍiʿatan", it would be correct. Al-Kisāʾī said: this is like the poet's saying:
ترى أرْبَاقَهُم متقلِّدِيهَا * إذا صَدِئ الحدِيدُ عَلَى الكُمَاةِ
(You see them wearing their tethers [around their necks] when the iron rusts upon the armoured warriors.)
But this does not resemble that, because the verb [i.e. participle] in al-mutaqallidīn already has a pronoun referring back to the tethers, so that became fit because of the returning pronoun. Similar to this is your saying "Your hand has not ceased — you stretching it out (bāsiṭahā)", because the action from you falls on the hand, so a pronoun referring back to what is at the beginning of the sentence is necessary. Had it been "fa-ẓallat aʿnāquhum lahā khāḍiʿīhā", this verse would be evidence for it. When you make a verb fall upon a noun and then annex it, you cannot make do with the verb of the annexed noun unless it agrees with the verb of the first; as in your saying "ʿAbd Allāh's hand has not ceased spending (munfiqan, masc.) and spending (munfiqatan, fem.)": this is of the agreeing kind «[Translator's note: manuscript folio marker 133b]», because you say "his hand is spending" and "he is spending". But it is not permissible to say "His hand was stretching (bāsiṭan)", because he is the one who stretches the hand and the hand is stretched; the action differs, and the action of one does not suffice for the other. If you repeat the mention of the hand, it is fit, and you say: "His hand has not ceased — he stretching it out (bāsiṭahā)".

farraa:7-7.t:
His saying: ﴿أَنبَتْنَا فِيهَا مِن كُلِّ زَوْجٍ كَرِيمٍ﴾ — He is saying: fine. It is said: it is as you say of a palm tree "noble (karīma)" when its fruit is good, or abundant; as one says of a ewe or a she-camel "karīma" when they give abundant milk. Al-Farrāʾ said: of every pair — of every kind.
His saying throughout this sūra: ﴿وَمَا كان أكثرهم مؤمِنِينَ﴾ — in the knowledge of Allah. He is saying: there is a sign for them in the Qurʾān and its revelation, but most of them, in the knowledge of Allah, will not believe.

farraa:11-11.t: His saying: ﴿قَوْمَ فِرْعَوْنَ أَلا يَتَّقُونَ﴾ — as for His saying ﴿أَلا يَتَّقُونَ﴾, had there been in its place "a-lā tattaqūn" it would be correct, because Mūsā was commanded to say to them "Will you not be God-fearing?" So the tāʾ would be permissible for Mūsā's addressing them; and the yāʾ is permissible because the revelation precedes the address. It is like Allah's saying ﴿قُلْ لِلَّذينَ كَفَرُوا سَتُغْلَبُونَ﴾ and ﴿سيُغْلَبونَ﴾.

farraa:13-13.t:
His saying: ﴿وَيَضِيقُ صَدْرِي﴾ — it is nominative because it is referred back to (أخاف). Had it been put in the accusative by referring it back to ﴿يُكَذبُونَ﴾, it would be a correct accusative. The [proper] way is the nominative, because he reported that his breast grows tight, and mentioned the defect that was in his tongue, and that is among the things he does not fear, because it already existed.
His saying: ﴿فَأَرْسِلْ إِلَىٰ هَارُونَ﴾ — he did not mention help or support; that is because the meaning is known, as you say "If something hateful befell me, I would send to you", meaning: that you might help me and succour me. When the meaning is known, what would make the speech concise is dropped from it.

farraa:19-19.t:
His saying: ﴿وَفَعَلْتَ فَعْلَتَكَ ٱلَّتِي فَعَلْتَ﴾ — [i.e.] his killing of the soul. The fāʾ of al-faʿla has fatḥa because it is a single instance, and when it is a single instance it is not fiʿla. Had it been meant like al-jilsa (manner of sitting) and al-mishya (gait), its kasra would be permissible. Abū al-ʿAbbās narrated to us, saying: Muḥammad narrated to us, saying: al-Farrāʾ narrated to us, saying: Mūsā al-Anṣārī narrated to me from al-Sarī ibn Ismāʿīl, from al-Shaʿbī, that he read ﴿وَفَعَلْتَ فَعْلَتَكَ﴾ with kasra on the fāʾ «[Translator's note: so in the source; the Arabic quotation is vowelled with fatḥa (فَعْلَتَكَ), although the reading described is fiʿlataka.]»; no one else read it so.
His saying: ﴿وَأَنتَ مِنَ ٱلْكَافِرِينَ﴾ — and you are now among those ungrateful for my favour, that is, for my rearing you. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is (قال فعلتها إذاً وأنا من الجَاهلين). "The astray" (al-ḍāllīn) and "the ignorant" (al-jāhilīn) may have one meaning, because you say "I was ignorant of the road" and "I strayed from it". Al-Farrāʾ said: when a thing is lost by you, you have aḍlaltahu.

farraa:21-21.t: His saying: ﴿فَوَهَبَ لِي رَبِّي حُكْماً﴾ — [i.e.] the Torah.

farraa:22-22.t:
His saying: ﴿وَتِلْكَ نِعْمَةٌ تَمُنُّهَا عَلَيَّ أَنْ عَبَّدتَّ﴾ — He is saying: it is — by my life — a favour, in that you reared me and did not enslave me as you enslaved the Children of Israel; and an indicates that. Similar to it in speech: you spare one of your two slaves from beating and beat the other, and the one spared says: "This is a favour to me, that you beat so-and-so and spared me." Then "and spared me" is dropped, while the meaning stands and is known. The Arabs say: ʿabbadtu al-ʿabīd and aʿbadtuhum (I enslaved them).
One of the Arabs recited to me:
علام يُعْبِدُنى قَومى وقد كثُرت * فيهم أبا عرُمَا شاءُوا وعِبْدانَ
(Why do my people treat me as a slave, when there are among them as many camels as they wish, and slaves?) «[Translator's note: the words «أبا عرُمَا» are corrupt in the source; probably «أباعرُ ما» (camels, as many as…).]»
(أن) may be nominative or accusative. The nominative is on [the sense of] your saying: "And that is a favour you remind me of: your enslavement of the Children of Israel"; and the accusative: "you remind me of it because of your enslaving the Children of Israel".

farraa:25-25.t: Someone may say: where is the answer to His saying ﴿ قَالَ لِمَنْ حَوْلَهُ أَلاَ تَسْتَمِعُونَ﴾? It is said: by His saying ﴿أَلاَ تَسْتَمِعُونَ﴾ he meant only: [listen] to the saying of Mūsā. So Mūsā replied, because he was the one meant by the answer, and said: [He is] the one to whose worship I call you.

farraa:26-28.t: His saying: ﴿رَبُّكُمْ وَرَبُّ آبَآئِكُمُ ٱلأَوَّلِينَ﴾ — and likewise His saying ﴿قَالَ رَبُّ ٱلْمَشْرِقِ وَٱلْمَغْرِبِ﴾ — he is saying: I call you to the worship of the Lord of the east and the west and what is between them.

farraa:51-51.t: His saying: ﴿أَن كُنَّآ أَوَّلَ ٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ — the proper way of the sentence is to give (أنْ) fatḥa, because it is past and it has the sense of a conditional. Had it been given kasra, with the jussive intended for what follows, it would be correct. His saying ﴿كُنَّآ أَوَّلَ ٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ — they are saying: the first of the believers among the people of our time.

farraa:54-54.t:
His saying: ﴿إِنَّ هَـٰؤُلاۤءِ لَشِرْذِمَةٌ قَلِيلُونَ﴾ — He is saying: a small band. [One says] qalīlūn and kathīrūn, but most of the speech of the Arabs is to say "Your people are few (qalīl)" and "our people are many (kathīr)". Qalīlūn and kathīrūn are permissible, good Arabic. It is permissible only because the fewness applies to all of them; so it was said qalīl, and qalīl was preferred over qalīlīn; and the plural was permissible since the fewness in meaning attaches to all of them, so their nouns appeared accordingly. Similar to it: "You are one tribe (ḥayy wāḥid)" and "ḥayy wāḥidūn", and the meaning of wāḥidūn is wāḥid, as al-Kumayt said:
فردّ قواصِىَ الأحيَاء منهم * قد رَجَعوا كحىّ وَاحِدِينا
(He brought back the far-flung clans of them, and they have returned like a single tribe.)

farraa:56-56.t: His saying: ﴿حَاذِرُونَ﴾ and ḥadhirūn — Abū al-ʿAbbās narrated to us, saying: Muḥammad narrated to us, saying: al-Farrāʾ narrated to us, saying: Abū Laylā al-Sijistānī narrated to me from Abū Jarīr, the judge of Sijistān, that Ibn Masʿūd read (وإنَّا لجَميِعٌ حَاذِرُونَ). They say [it means]: fully equipped (muʾdūn) with weapons; He is saying: possessing equipment of weapons. And ﴿حذِرُونَ﴾ [is also read]. It is as though al-ḥādhir is the one who is wary of you now, and al-ḥadhir is the one created wary, whom you never meet except wary.
